concerns.text: US-2's independent test requires verifying that k_est 'correlates linearly with the ground-truth friction coefficient across a sweep of multiple randomized trials', but no FR or SC covers estimator validation against ground truth. FR-001 only defines computation; SC-002 only measures downstream success rate. Add an FR/SC for the correlation-validation experiment or the story's core testable claim is unbacked.

FR-007 anchors to '(See Edge Cases)' rather than a user story. Its scope (clamping k_est for numerical stability) plainly serves US-2's estimator, so re-anchor it to US-2 (and/or US-1 via FR-002's reward scaling) for clean traceability.

concerns.location: spec.md:FR-001 vs Edge Cases (stiction) vs Assumptions
concerns.text: FR-001 restricts k_est computation to the sliding regime ('at every simulation timestep in the sliding regime (|Δv_object| > 0)'), but the Edge Cases section mandates an epsilon (1e-4) denominator when Δv_object is 'effectively zero (stiction)', and Assumptions says stiction 'is handled by the epsilon clamping in FR-007' — yet FR-007 contains no epsilon clause (only output clamping). Three mutually incompatible statements about stiction handling; pick one mechanism and reference it consistently.

US-1 Scenario 2 says low friction must demonstrate 'the estimator correctly identifies low stiffness and reduces detachment penalties', but FR-002 specifies that for k_est < 0.2 the system decreases r_contact (contact maintenance), not r_detach. The low-stiffness adaptation target contradicts itself between story and FR.

FR-001 (the stiffness-proxy estimator) is anchored '(See US-1)' but the estimator is the subject of US-2 ('Virtual Tactile Stiffness Estimation'); US-1 is zero-shot adaptation. FR-006 correctly anchors to US-2 for the same estimator. Fix the cross-reference.

concerns.location: spec.md:US-1 title/body vs rest of document
concerns.text: Terminology drifts between 'damping' (US-1 title 'Zero-Shot Adaptation to Unseen Damping', idea/constitution) and 'friction' (all scenarios, FR-003, edge cases). The spec never states these are the same property; pick one term or define the mapping.
Typo: 'bounded by a small lower threshold and a large upper limit. to prevent numerical instability' — stray period and lowercase 'to'.

FR-007 requires clamping k_est 'to a physically meaningful positive range bounded by a small lower threshold and a large upper limit' — neither bound is defined, so an implementer cannot know when the requirement is met. The Edge Cases section likewise says 'clamp the output to a defined range' without defining it. State the numeric bounds (or the procedure that fixes them, e.g., 'clamped to [1e-4, 10]') so the clamp is deterministically checkable.

'verify that the computed k_est correlates linearly with the ground-truth friction coefficient' states no evaluation criterion — no correlation measure, threshold, or judged procedure. Specify e.g. Pearson r ≥ some value across the sweep, or an explicit visual/regression inspection procedure, so the test has a pass/fail condition.

'a diverse set of novel articulated object geometries' is not verifiable — no count or diversity criterion. The idea doc specifies 10 novel objects; state the count (or a generation procedure with pinned seed) so FR-003 can be checked.

SC-003/SC-004 defer to 'the free-tier CI runner's time limit' and 'the RAM constraint of the target environment' without naming the reference values. US-3 already fixes ≤6 hours and 7GB — cite those explicit limits in the SCs so the measurement reference is unambiguous.

The kicked-back concern about normal-force confounding is unaddressed: in the sliding regime torque ~ mu*N*r, so k_est = |Δτ|/|Δv| may track contact load rather than stiffness. No FR or scenario requires controlling/measuring normal force, and the US-2 independent test (correlate k_est with ground-truth friction) cannot distinguish a load confound. Add a requirement to log or control normal force (or justify why the confound is inert) so the construct validity of the Virtual Tactile proxy is testable.

The zero-shot domain shift is undefined. Scenario 1 says 'randomized friction (0.8–1.2) not seen during training' but no FR pins the TRAINING friction range or a mechanism guaranteeing test objects are disjoint from it. Without this, the 'zero-shot' claim in the idea's research question cannot be validated. Add an FR defining the training distribution and the disjointness check for the NovelObjectSet.

The idea's methodology explicitly acquires the 277 DragMesh-2 trajectories and generates 10 novel objects; the spec only says 'a diverse set of novel articulated object geometries' and never mentions the base dataset acquisition. The sample-size assumption hand-waves 'a sample size of novel objects is sufficient'. Name the base dataset (DragMesh-2 trajectories) as an input and state the planned novel-object count or the power analysis that will set it.

The normal-force confound flagged at the prior stage remains unaddressed. In the sliding regime, hand torque is dominated by Coulomb friction (τ ≈ μ·N·r), so k_est = |Δτ|/|Δv| will track contact load and friction, not stiffness. The spec's Assumptions assert the proxy is valid 'in the sliding regime' but offers no control for, or measurement of, normal force N. Construct validity of the entire 'Virtual Tactile' mechanism is broken unless FR-001 is revised (e.g., normalize by estimated normal force, or reframe k_est explicitly as a friction/resistance proxy rather than stiffness).

The 'zero-shot' claim is not supported by the design. The spec randomizes friction 0.1–1.2 for novel objects (Methodology/US-1) and tests at 0.8–1.2, but never defines the training friction distribution or a mechanism guaranteeing test objects lie outside it. If training and test friction ranges overlap, 'unseen damping conditions' is false and SC-001 measures in-distribution robustness, not zero-shot adaptation. The spec must define the training distribution and require test friction values strictly outside it (or rename the claim).

Thresholds k_est > 1.0 and k_est < 0.2 are dimensionally meaningless: k_est = |Δτ|/|Δv| carries units (N·m·s/m) whose magnitude depends on joint and object scales. A fixed numeric cutoff cannot generalize across objects/geometries. The spec should require a normalized or per-object-calibrated k_est before threshold-based reward scaling, or define the thresholds relative to a reference distribution.

A paired t-test on binary success-rate outcomes across ~10 novel objects is statistically mismatched: per-object success rates are proportions from few episodes, the pairing unit is ill-defined (episodes vs objects), and n≈10 gives negligible power for a 15% effect. Use a mixed-effects logistic regression or paired test on per-object proportions with an arcsine/logit transform and a power analysis; the Assumption that n is 'sufficient' is asserted, not justified.

US-2's validation test checks that k_est 'correlates linearly with the ground-truth friction coefficient' — but the spec elsewhere calls k_est a stiffness proxy. If the ground truth for validation is friction while the construct is stiffness, the validation target and the construct are mismatched; if k_est is actually a friction proxy, FR-002's 'stiffness' framing and reward-scaling rationale must be restated. Pick one construct and validate against its matching ground truth.

responses.response: Fixed FR‑003 to require exactly 10 novel articulated objects, matching the idea document.

responses.what_changed: Created FR-010 and referenced it in US‑1 Scenario 1; updated FR‑003 accordingly.

new_concerns.text: SC-001 still contains a '[deferred]' placeholder for the required improvement margin. A success criterion must specify a concrete, measurable threshold (e.g., “≥ 15 % higher success rate than the static baseline”) or a reproducible procedure for determining the margin; otherwise the criterion is not testable.

SC-002 also uses a '[deferred]' placeholder for the required improvement over the static‑reward baseline. The criterion must provide a quantitative target (e.g., “≥ 10 % higher success rate”) or a defined statistical test so that compliance can be objectively verified.
